newsitem.title: HUNGARY: CHIRAC HAS SWEET WORDS FOR HUNGARY ON EU ENTRY.
newsitem.headline: CHIRAC HAS SWEET WORDS FOR HUNGARY ON EU ENTRY.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac ended a two-day state visit having told the Hungarians exactly what they wanted to hear -- that there is no reason they should not be in the European Union by the year 2000.

"I want your country to join the European Union in the year 2000 -- France will do everything to ensure that date is respected," he told a gathering of Hungarian MPs, officials and dignatories in Hungary's parliament.

Hungary's Prime Minister Gyula Horn said last month he hoped European Union membership could be achieved by the end of the year 2000 but EU experts have said that deadline is unrealistic and it will probably take at least two years longer for the first former communist Central European states to join.
To warm applause, Chirac said such a target date was achievable if everyone "made the necessary efforts".
The French president also proposed the setting up of a European conference to bring together the 15 EU members and the 11 applicant countires.
"We fully agree with President Chirac's target and we also agree with the idea of a plenary conference," a smiling Horn told reporters prior to Chirac's departure on Friday.
Chirac also had a message for Hungarian commentators who expressed fears that he was raising false expectations.
"I do not wish to raise false hopes -- what is needed is ambitions and the will," he said, adding that target date was shared by Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany.
The French president also expressed his "unqualified support" for Hungary's application to join NATO, which he described as a historic opportunity to "bring together the European family".
But he warned that the enlargement of NATO must be well prepared in advance with due regard for Russia's sensitivities.
"(The enlargement) must be done in a way which does not give Russia the sentiment of being humiliated or confronted," he said.
The message will not be lost on the Russians, who in recent weeks have hardened their stance against NATO expansion and who themselves are due to play host to Chirac in two weeks' time.

Diplomats said before the trip to Hungary Chirac was anxious to erase the negative image of France created across Central and Eastern Europe by his predecessor Francois Mitterrand's statement after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
Mitterand said that it would be "decades" before the first former Communist states joined the EU.

That statement, and early French resistance to removing barriers to imports especially of farm produce from those countries, cast Paris in the eyes of many east Europeans as the main adversary of their entry into the EU "rich men's club".

Chirac's enthusiastic advocacy of early EU entry may have gone some way to correcting that impression, but he won over the hearts as well as the minds of many Hungarians by awarding Legion d'Honneur decorations to their popular president Arpad Goncz and 12 other veterans of the 1956 uprising.
Several thousands Hungarians were killed when Soviet troops invaded Hungary in November 1956 to crush the anti-Stalinist insurrection. Goncz spent six years in jail for his part in the events.
"For us to receive these decorations we needed to stay alive and in order to stay alive others had to give their lives," Goncz said on receiving his medal.
